questions.question: Which of the following best explains why adding extra information such as tables or graphical models to natural‑language requirements improves the specification of a system like an insulin pump?

options.A: It reduces the need for stakeholder interviews.
options.B: It clarifies how computations proceed and how the system state changes.
options.C: It eliminates the need for use case diagrams.
options.D: It replaces the need for any textual description.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Adding tables or graphical models helps show computation flow, state changes, and interaction sequences, as described on page 24.  

---

questions.question: When elaborating a scenario, which element is most likely to be added after the initial outline to ensure that error handling is covered?

options.A: A description of the system’s initial state.
options.B: A description of what can go wrong and how problems are handled.
options.C: A list of all possible actors.
options.D: A diagram of the user interface layout.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] The scenario components include a description of what can go wrong and its handling (page 19).  

---

questions.question: In a use case diagram, how are the entities that interact with the system (human or other systems) represented?

options.A: As rectangles labeled with the system name.
options.D: As shaded ellipses called use cases.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Actors are shown as stick figures in a use case diagram (page 25).  

---

questions.question: Which statement most accurately reflects the relationship between a “scenario” and a “use case” as described in the provided material?

options.A: A scenario is a high‑level diagram, while a use case is a textual description.
options.B: A scenario details a single interaction flow, whereas a use case groups many possible interactions.
options.C: A scenario and a use case are synonymous terms used interchangeably.
options.D: A scenario only describes error conditions, while a use case only describes normal flow.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Scenarios outline a specific interaction (including normal flow, errors, etc.) and are used to flesh out the broader set of interactions captured by use cases (pages 19‑25).  

---

questions.question: If a development team wants to illustrate how multiple activities can occur concurrently during a scenario, which part of the scenario description should they focus on expanding?

options.A: The description of the system state at the start.
options.C: Information about other activities that might be happening at the same time.
options.D: The final system state when the scenario ends.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Concurrent activities are captured in the scenario element that describes “other activities that might be going on at the same time” (page 19).  

---

questions.question: Consider an insulin pump specification that uses a tabular format to show computation steps. Which advantage does this tabular specification provide over a purely narrative description?

options.A: It eliminates the need for any user testing.
options.B: It allows readers to quickly compare input‑output relationships for each step.
options.C: It automatically generates use case diagrams.
options.D: It hides the internal logic from stakeholders.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Tables make it easier to see how computations proceed and how inputs map to outputs, as noted on page 24.  

---

questions.question: Which of the following would NOT be considered an actor in a UML use case diagram according to the context?

options.A: A nurse operating the insulin pump.
options.B: The insulin pump’s internal control algorithm.
options.C: An external monitoring system that receives data.
options.D: A software developer writing code for the pump.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Remember | Difficulty: Easy] Actors are entities that interact with the system (human or other systems); a developer writing code is not an interacting actor in the operational sense (page 25).  

---

questions.question: When constructing a use case diagram, what is the purpose of linking actors to ellipses representing interactions?

options.A: To show inheritance relationships among actors.
options.B: To indicate which actors initiate or participate in each interaction.
options.C: To define the sequence of steps within the use case.
options.D: To assign priority levels to each use case.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Easy] Lines connect actors with the named ellipses to show participation in the interaction (page 25).  

---

questions.question: A scenario includes a description of the system state when it ends. Why is this element important for system designers?

options.A: It determines the graphical layout of the user interface.
options.B: It provides a baseline for verifying that the system reached the expected final condition.
options.C: It specifies the programming language to be used.
options.D: It lists all possible error messages the system may display.

questions.explanation:
[Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Knowing the final system state helps designers verify that the scenario completed as intended (page 19).  

---

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates how a use case diagram contributes to requirements engineering?

options.A: It replaces all textual requirements with visual symbols.
options.B: It provides a high‑level view of all possible user‑system interactions, aiding completeness checks.
options.C: It details the internal class structure of the system.
options.D: It defines the exact sequence of method calls for each feature.

questions.explanation: [Bloom: Understand | Difficulty: Medium] Use case diagrams give a high‑level representation of interactions, ensuring that the set of use cases covers the required functionality (page 25).
